events.title: Laban's sons resent Jacob's wealth
events.narrative_summary: Jacob hears Laban's sons say that he has taken all that was their father's. He also sees that Laban's face is no longer toward him as before.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Jacob's twenty years with Laban (31:38, 41) are 14 for the wives, ending with Joseph's birth, and 6 for the flock (31:41). The scene is about 6 years after evt.gen_30.joseph_born, so I anchor on its END with a 6-year offset and a 1-year margin. No hour or day is named; REGNAL_YEAR because the twenty-year count frames it.
events.ancient_year_marker: In the twentieth year of his service

events.title: Yahweh tells Jacob to return to his fathers' land
events.narrative_summary: Yahweh tells Jacob to go back to the land of his fathers and to his kindred, and promises to be with him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No time word. It follows the sons' complaint and Laban's cooled face directly; a margin of 3 days, no gap. REGNAL_YEAR as the scene falls under the twenty-year frame.

events.title: Jacob persuades Rachel and Leah to leave
events.narrative_summary: Jacob calls Rachel and Leah to the field and tells them of Laban's deceit and of God's call to return. They answer that they have no share left in their father's house and tell him to do what God has said.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'Jacob sent and called' (31:4) follows the divine word; I put it 1 day after, with a 3-day margin (he needs to send a message to the women and meet them in the field). The scene lasts about 2 hours. REGNAL_YEAR as the scene falls under the twenty-year frame.

events.title: Jacob flees from Laban with his family and flocks
events.narrative_summary: While Laban is away shearing his sheep, Rachel steals the household gods and Jacob, deceiving Laban, takes wives, children and all his livestock across the river toward Gilead.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Jacob leaves while Laban is at the shearing (31:19), 3 days off (30:36). I put it 1 day after the council, margin 2 days. The event is the departure itself (1 day); the journey that follows is carried by the dated events: Laban is told 3 days later and overtakes Jacob in Gilead about 10 days after the start (31:22-25). The road Paddan to Gilead is about 754 km (donkey 23 days, army 41 days); the text's count is shorter and wins. DAY_SEQUENCE because the following days are counted.
events.ancient_season_marker: While Laban went to shear his sheep

events.title: Laban learns on the third day that Jacob has fled
events.narrative_summary: On the third day Laban is told that Jacob has fled.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'On the third day' (31:22), counted inclusively: Jacob's start day is the first day, so the report falls on the third, an offset of 2 days from the flight's START, with margin of 12 hours. Rashi: there was a three-day journey between them. DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Laban pursues Jacob for seven days
events.narrative_summary: Laban takes his kinsmen and pursues Jacob a seven days' journey, overtaking him in the hill country of Gilead.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts when he hears (END of laban_told); 'a seven days' journey' (31:23) is the duration, with 12 hours margin. Rashi says the seven days are the distance Laban covered in a day while Jacob travelled seven; Rashbam says Jacob went slowly. DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: God warns Laban in a dream not to harm Jacob
events.narrative_summary: God comes to Laban the Aramean in a dream by night and tells him to take care not to speak to Jacob either good or bad.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'By night' (31:24), and Laban calls it 'yesternight' in 31:29, so it is the night before the overtaking. Placed 6 days after the pursuit began at the middle watch (22:00), 12 hours margin; the hour is my reading. DIURNAL_HOUR on the 'night' marker.

events.title: Laban overtakes Jacob in the hill country of Gilead
events.narrative_summary: Laban overtakes Jacob, who has pitched his tent in the hill country; Laban and his kinsmen camp in the hill country of Gilead.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts at the END of the pursuit, the arrival being the end of the 7 days. The hour is not named, so the margin is 6 hours. DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Laban accuses Jacob of stealing away and taking his gods
events.narrative_summary: Laban asks Jacob why he fled secretly with his daughters, without a farewell, and why he stole his gods.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A speech directly following the overtaking, about 20 minutes. Treated as the same day; margin 6 hours. DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Jacob answers and curses the thief with death
events.narrative_summary: Jacob answers that he feared Laban would take his daughters, and says that whoever has the gods shall not live. Not knowing that Rachel stole them, he invites Laban to search.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A short speech after the accusation, about 10 minutes; same day. DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Laban searches the tents; Rachel hides the gods
events.narrative_summary: Laban searches the tents of Jacob, Leah and the two maidservants, and then Rachel's. She has put the household gods in the camel's saddle and sits on them, saying she cannot rise because she is in her monthly period.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Four tents in a camp: about 3 hours, with 1 hour margin. Same day as the accusation. DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Jacob angrily rebukes Laban for twenty years of wrongs
events.narrative_summary: Jacob, angry, asks what his offence was; he recounts twenty years of faithful service, of loss from wild beasts, of heat and cold and sleeplessness, and of Laban changing his wages ten times, and says that only God's help kept him from being sent away empty.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the failed search directly; a speech of about 20 minutes. The 'twenty years' (31:38, 41) is the same count as in the anchor of the chapter's first event. DAY_SEQUENCE.
events.ancient_year_marker: Twenty years I have been in your house

events.title: Laban answers and proposes a covenant
events.narrative_summary: Laban answers that daughters, children and flocks are his, yet what can he do about them today? He proposes that they make a covenant to be a witness between them.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows directly; a short speech of about 10 minutes, same day. DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Jacob and Laban make a covenant with a pillar and a heap
events.narrative_summary: Jacob sets up a stone as a pillar and his kinsmen make a heap. Laban calls it Jegar-sahadutha and Jacob Galeed; it is also called Mizpah, and Laban sets the terms: no harming the daughters, no other wives, no crossing the heap to harm. Laban calls on the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor to judge between them, and Jacob swears by the Fear of his father Isaac.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Stones, a heap and an oath: about 3 hours after the proposal; same day. The meal and the night of 31:54 follow. DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Jacob offers a sacrifice and they eat and stay the night
events.narrative_summary: Jacob offers a sacrifice on the mountain and calls his kinsmen to eat bread. They eat and spend the night on the mountain.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'Tarried all night' (31:54): the feast and the night run about 13 hours from the end of the covenant so that the END falls at daybreak (about 06:00), since the departure follows 'early in the morning' (31:55 = Hebrew 32:1). Margin 2 hours. DAY_SEQUENCE.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: They tarried all night in the mountain

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Laban's proposal is carried out by the pillar, heap and oath (31:44-53).
Because God warned him, Laban says he could have harmed Jacob but speaks only an accusation (31:24, 29).
Rachel and Leah agree to do whatever God has told him (31:16), and Jacob rises and sets his family on camels (31:17).
Laban is told on the third day that Jacob has fled (31:22).
After Jacob's rebuke Laban turns from accusation to a proposal of covenant (31:43-44).
Laban's charge that his gods were stolen leads to the search of the tents (31:30-33).
The seven days' pursuit ends when Laban overtakes Jacob in Gilead (31:23, 25).
The sons' words and Laban's changed face make Jacob consult his wives about leaving (31:1-5).
Having heard of the flight, Laban takes his kinsmen and pursues (31:23).
Yahweh's command to return to his fathers' land (31:3) is carried out when Jacob sets out with all he has (31:17-18).

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'gal' (heap of stones); Laban's Aramaic name Jegar-sahadutha and Jacob's Hebrew Galeed both mean 'heap of witness'.
entities.summary_bio: The heap of stones Jacob's kinsmen gather and pile up (31:46). They eat beside it, and Laban declares it a witness between him and Jacob (31:48).

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'matstsevah', a standing stone. The name Mizpah ('watchtower') is tied to the pillar in 31:49 in some readings.
entities.summary_bio: A stone Jacob sets up as a pillar (31:45) at the covenant site with Laban. Laban speaks of it as one he has cast up (31:51), and it stands as a witness that neither will cross the line for harm (31:52).

entities.etymology_meaning: Of uncertain origin; the plural 'teraphim' names household images, which some scholars link to ancestor or inheritance claims.
entities.summary_bio: Household images that belonged to Laban. Rachel steals them while Laban is away shearing (31:19), hides them in her camel's saddlebag and sits on them when Laban searches (31:34-35). Laban calls them 'my gods' (31:30), and Jacob, not knowing the theft, swears death on whoever has them (31:32).

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'gamal', camel; no further etymology is offered.
entities.summary_bio: The camels on which Jacob sets his sons and wives for the flight from Laban (31:17). Rachel hides the household gods in a camel's saddlebag (31:34).

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'ach' (brother) used broadly for male relatives and companions.
entities.summary_bio: The relatives and retainers of Jacob whom he tells to gather stones for the heap (31:46) and whom he invites to the sacrificial meal on the mountain (31:54). The text does not name them.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'ach' (brother) used broadly for male relatives and clansmen.
entities.summary_bio: The relatives Laban takes with him when he pursues Jacob for seven days (31:23). They camp with him in Gilead and witness the confrontation and the covenant.

entities.etymology_meaning: 'Heap of witness'; Mizpah means 'watchtower', from Laban's saying 'the LORD watch between me and you' (31:49).
entities.summary_bio: The site in the hill country of Gilead where Jacob and Laban make their covenant, named for the cairn of witness (31:47-49). It marks the line neither will cross for harm.

components.evidence_explanation: 31:48 has Laban say the heap is a witness between them this day.
31:47-48 gives the names Jegar-sahadutha (Laban) and Galeed (Jacob).
31:36 says it burned to Jacob and he quarreled with Laban.
31:44-52 shows the covenant proposed and sealed with pillar and heap.

components.label_value: Camped in the hill country of Gilead
components.evidence_explanation: 31:25 says Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country when Laban overtook him.
31:2 says Laban's face was not toward Jacob as it had been before.
31:52 calls the pillar a witness between Jacob and Laban.
31:19 says Rachel stole them; 31:34 shows them in her saddlebag.

systems.name: Conditional curse of death
systems.ancient_near_east_context: A speaker pronounces a penalty on whoever is found guilty, in front of witnesses, and the verdict is left to the inquiry. Such oath-curses bind the speaker to carry out the penalty.
rules_and_mechanics: The curse names no one; it falls on 'whoever' is found with the stolen object.
It is spoken in front of kinsmen who serve as witnesses (31:32).
The inquiry is held in the presence of both parties' relatives.

systems.name: Household gods (teraphim)
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Small household images kept by Mesopotamian and West Semitic families. Texts from Nuzi are often cited to suggest a link to inheritance, though that is debated; the teraphim are also associated with divination and household protection.
rules_and_mechanics: The images belong to the household's head and are kept in his house.
Taking them is treated as theft of the owner's gods (31:30).
Women's uncleanness is an accepted reason to stay seated and not stand before a man (31:35).

systems.name: Witness monument
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Stones, pillars and heaps were set up in the region to witness agreements and mark boundaries, with a god invoked as watcher over the line.
rules_and_mechanics: A standing stone and a heap of stones are raised together at the site (31:45-46).
The monument is given a name in each party's language (31:47).
Neither party will cross the line for harm (31:52).
The deities of both sides are called on to judge any breach (31:49, 31:53).

system_instances.outcome_summary: Jacob tells his wives that in a dream the angel of God showed him the striped, speckled and mottled he-goats mating, and said that God had seen Laban's treatment of him.
system_instances.significance_note: It grounds Jacob's wealth in God's action, and the angel's closing order to return gives his wives a divine reason to leave.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Laban invokes the LORD as watcher between them, then the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor as judges.
system_instances.significance_note: Because the two parties will be out of sight of each other, God is called to enforce the terms.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Jacob's kinsmen gather stones into a heap and eat there beside it.
system_instances.significance_note: A shared meal at the heap is a typical sealing of a treaty.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Laban and Jacob make a covenant: neither will cross the heap and pillar for harm, and Jacob must not mistreat Laban's daughters or take other wives.
system_instances.significance_note: It ends the pursuit peacefully and fixes the line between Aram and Jacob's lands.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Jacob offers a sacrifice on the mountain and invites his kinsmen to eat. They stay the night there.
system_instances.significance_note: It closes the covenant with an offering and a meal before Jacob and Laban part.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Jacob swears by the Fear of his father Isaac.
system_instances.significance_note: He answers Laban's two gods with an oath by Isaac's God alone.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Jacob declares that whoever is found with Laban's gods shall not live, not knowing that Rachel took them.
system_instances.significance_note: The curse puts Rachel unknowingly at risk and adds tension to the search.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God comes to Laban in a night dream and tells him not to speak to Jacob either good or bad.
system_instances.significance_note: It restrains Laban and explains why the confrontation ends in a covenant and not in violence.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Jacob raises a pillar and his kinsmen pile a heap of stones, and both are named witnesses between the two men.
system_instances.significance_note: It supplies the place-name Galeed and a fixed boundary marker.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD tells Jacob to return to the land of his fathers and kindred, promising to be with him.
system_instances.significance_note: It starts the departure and places the whole flight under divine direction.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Rachel puts the gods in a camel's saddlebag and sits on them, saying she cannot rise because of her period. Laban searches the tent and finds nothing.
system_instances.significance_note: Rachel's deception shows the household-god scheme working and turns the search into a failed accusation, which gives Jacob his protest in 31:36-42.

system_instances.outcome_summary: While Laban is away shearing, Rachel steals her father's household gods.
system_instances.significance_note: The theft sets up Laban's accusation and the search scene, and the text gives no reason for it.

edges.description: Jacob declares that whoever has the gods shall not live; the thief is Rachel.
Jacob 'steals the heart' of Laban by fleeing without telling him.
Jacob angrily asks what his offence is after the fruitless search.
Jacob offers a sacrifice on the mountain after the covenant.
Jacob sends for Leah to meet him at his flock in the field.
Jacob sends for Rachel to meet him at his flock in the field.
Jacob swears by the Fear of Isaac to keep the terms.
Laban charges Jacob with stealing away and with stealing his gods.
Laban catches up with Jacob in the hill country of Gilead.
Laban invites Jacob to make a covenant to serve as a witness between them.
Laban takes his kinsmen and chases Jacob for seven days.
Rachel hides the gods under her and claims she cannot rise, so Laban's search fails.
Rachel takes her father's household gods while he is away shearing.
The LORD tells Jacob to return to the land of his fathers and kindred.
God warns Laban in a dream not to speak to Jacob from good to bad.
